legislation any possibility for excusing ourselves or giving any excuse to anyone else so they can claim they were acting on the basis of some matter of lawful sanctions. I am concerned about that phrase and my colleague, who brought this to my attention, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), will be presenting an amendment in this regard. I hope that Members on the government side will consider very carefully that amendment.
I would like to conclude my remarks by commending the presentation of this Bill. I know our Party is fully behind the Bill itself in general. I urge all Hon. Members to consider the amendment which will be made by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre, later on.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to stand in the House today in support of this legislation on behalf of my Party, thereby joining with,
I am sure, all Hon. Members in the passing of legislation which allows Canada to fulfil its international commitments by giving legislative effect to the United Nations convention for the protection of all persons subjected to torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment.
This is an issue which has a considerable history, but not a long history. The concern about torture in this world and the development of a consensus of the need for its elimination really developed rather late. If one looks back to the development of the declaration in this convention, one sees that it first arose during the 1960s and 1970s when there was concern about reports of torture in southern Asia, Africa, South America, eastern Europe and elsewhere.
Giving a more dramatic effect to the concern, there followed the Bertrand Russell tribunal which examined the situation in Chile, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. The tribunal reached the conclusion that torture constituted a crime against humanity. Since that time Canada has been actively engaged in furthering the development of an international system and convention. Its purpose would be the elimination of torture and the punishment of those who inflict torture. It was a part of the special working group of the Human Rights Commission in 1977. It was the first to sign a unilateral declaration in 1982. In 1983, it cosponsored a resolution according the highest priority to the development of an international declaration and convention. The convention which ultimately resulted was open for signature on February 4, 1985, and Canada signed in August of that year. Canada was among the few nations to provide financing to the UN Voluntary Fund for the Victims of Torture. Canada has consistently provided leadership. This Bill is not only a reflection of Canada's international humanitarian and human rights obligations, it also provides a legislative base for the implementation of appropriate sanctions to implement Section 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which asserts that everyone has the right not to be subjected to any unusual or cruel treatment or punishment.
Criminal Code
The convention calls upon the signatory states to develop legislation which provides for the criminalization of torture, as well as acts which comprise complicity or participation in torture. This Bill does that. Torture is defined as inflicting severe pain or suffering upon persons, or inflicting severe pain or suffering which results from omission, by an agent of government for reasons of punishment, coercion, intimidation or to obtain information. There is another reason for which torture may not be inflicted which is specified, and that is by reason of discrimination. That is included in the convention and in the legislation and certainly calls attention to the widespread use of torture and other activities which inflict pain on a considerable number of people in South Africa.
The first requirement, that is the criminalization of torture of a mental or a physical sort, is provided for in the legislation. The second requirement is that it be given universal jurisdiction. Torture inflicted by Canadians, imposed by Canadians, or torture inflicted by someone who is in Canada, even if that act took place elsewhere, is subject to prosecution. It also covers acts of torture if it occurs on Canadian ships or aircraft and provides for extradition in appropriate cases and, if extradition is inappropriate, calls for prosecution here.
Further, the convention sets out that there can be no justification for torture, that it is not an excuse to state that torture was inflicted by the order of a superior officer. It also provides that if evidence is provided or statements are made by virtue of the pain inflicted through torture, then they cannot be considered as legal evidence in any proceeding.
In those respects the legislation meets the requirements of the international convention in a legislative way. But when one praises the Government for introducing this legislation, which will surely pass, we have to be conscious of the other requirements that the declaration requires to be met. First, when one considers the requirement that acts of torture be prosecuted, that they not go unpunished, let us not reach the conclusion that we refer only to situations that may occur elsewhere. Of course, Canada is not a nation that has been accused of the use of punishment or torture in ways which are condemned in the universal convention or its preceding declaration. However, there are situations in which torture has been alleged although not proved.
If one refers to an additional aspect of the universal convention, it states that member states are obliged to prevent other acts of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment that do not amount to torture. All one has to do is recall the situation some years ago at Archambault Prison where it became evident, as it has all too often become evident in the past, that when allegations of torture or mistreatment are made against the police we are faced with extreme difficulty in proving them. We are all too often faced with a situation in which those who are accused of torture, cruel punishment or inhuman punishment, are the very people, the very groups, the very agencies to whom the allegations are

Criminal Code
made. It seems to me in looking at the implementation of this legislation domestically that one has to consider that provision has to be made for the independent examination of allegations, apart from the police or others who may be involved directly, in order to provide those people who make such claims have an opportunity to have their claims properly heard. All too often, and most notably in instances where native people or visible minority groups make allegations of mistreatment, such allegations are left unsatisfied because we do not have the mechanisms by which such allegations may be properly heard by an independent body in which trust can be had.
I note, too, that the international convention provides that there should be compensation for victims of torture, that they should have an enforceable right of fair and adequate compensation, including the means for full rehabilitation, to the extent that that is possible. I hope that in the discussions that are to occur with the provinces the right of those who prove themselves to be victims of torture will be specifically addressed, and that they be compensated for whatever harm has been inflicted upon them.
I hope that we will have a report from governments, federal and provincial, of the extent to which those governments have met another requirement of the convention. I refer to the implementation of administrative, judicial, legislative and other measures to ensure that all who are responsible, whether they be police officers, police forces, military personnel or any others who may be involved in the arrest, detention or imprisonment of Canadian citizens, will be well-informed of the requirements of the legislation that we are discussing today, and that an active effort be made to educate them about the limits of their power and the sanctions that will be imposed upon them if they violate the legislation which we have before us. If there is any prescription for the failure of legislation of this sort, it is not to provide clear directions, a statement of clear regulations and the education of those who might be involved in situations in which torture may occur.
1 am proud that Canada has exercised leadership in the area of this international covenant. But I must take note of the fact that when, in 1985, the declaration was approved by the United Nations, there was absolute unanimity within that body in favour of its adoption. However, if we look at the record revealed in reports of Amnesty International we find that 67 nations, more than one-third of the membership of the United Nations, are nations about which allegations of torture, cruelty and inhuman punishment have been made. There is within that fact a great deal of hypocrisy. Some of the nations are well known for their violations of human rights in general, for the inappropriate detention of prisoners and for cruel and inhuman punishment and torture. South Africa leads the list in that regard. Surely, El Salvador, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, South Korea, the U.S.S.R., Israel and Saudi Arabia provide us with a spectrum of nations that are involved in this inhumane treatment of humankind.
Thus we are drawn to another consideration with respect to Canada's implementation of its strong concern about torture.
It is to examine closely the kinds of relations this Government has with countries which have clear records of vicious treatment of their own citizens. It seems to me that torture is not that frequent in Canada; this is an empty piece of legislation unless we are able to also implement other measures that will show the world our utter contempt for those who would torture their own citizens, whether in war or in peace, whether for intimidation or because of race. So we should be looking systematically at the human rights records of the countries of the world with which our Government has relations. The Congress of the United States does it. The Americans have a complete listing, and examine human rights situations including false imprisonment, torture, and other inhumane acts. This provides a basis by which policy in respect of those governments can be directed.
When it comes to the provision of aid, the records of those nations should be available to us to determine in what manner, in what form, to whom, and whether we will provide aid. It is significant that we are not only unaware of what nations the Government considers it appropriate to have dealings with, but we do not know to what nations our country sells arms. In many cases that puts Canada in a position where we place guns in the hands of those who kill, maim, and torture their citizens. If we are to live up to our responsibilities in that regard, we must move beyond this legislation. Then we will have met our obligations.
When we look at those who come within our borders, whether they be diplomats such as the Ambassador from Sri Lanka or ordinary people of no particular notoriety, we should examine their records to see whether they have been involved in the imposition of torture. If that is so, we should either put them in jail or tell them to go home where they will be tried for their crimes. Only with complete involvement in ensuring that torturers will be punished will we have fulfilled our international obligations and our obligations to the consciences of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) spoke on the Bill. He indicated our general position of support for it and our commitment to a large role by Canada in pursuing internationally the elimination of torture.
The reason I wanted to speak was that in my political career I have had fair experience in the workings of the United Nations. When the United Nations is unanimous about anything, I tend to worry. When I was first introduced to this dossier, including the Bill, I took a look at some of the details of the negotiations of the United Nations, of the treaty reached, and of the Bill now before the House. I want to say unequivocally, as did the Hon. Member for Eglinton- Lawrence, that the Bill and the debate which took place at the United Nations represent a step forward in the elimination of torture in the world.
March 26, 1987

I do not want to indicate that we have any reservations about what the new Government has done at the United Nations and here by bringing forward the Bill in compliance with the terms of the convention which it signed. However, I suggest that there is a very serious shortcoming in the convention signed at the United Nations and in the Bill before us. 1 do not want to suggest that we should have objected to the convention when it was negotiated at the United Nations. I can almost take it for granted that Canada would have been one of the nations pressing hardest for effective measures to reduce torture and eliminate torture in all parts of the world.
However, the Bill before us could be better. When we reach the stage of clause by clause consideration in Committee of the Whole, which I hope will be in a few minutes, I will propose an amendment. I think the principle is important enough to mention it now.
The United Nations is famous for intentional ambiguities. The ambiguities are intentional because in many cases without ambiguity in the measures brought forward by the United Nations there would not be consensus. It gets agreement among a large number of states because one group has a certain interpretation of what it is doing, while another group has another interpretation. The basic consensus at the United Nations about torture is a step forward, but the Bill before us does not go as far as it should.
When we in Canada talk about domestic legislation, we should set an example in the legislation that we bring forward. It might inspire some of the other countries that signed the convention to bring a forthcoming, unequivocal Bill before their own Parliaments and legislatures to provide real measures for dealing with torture and torturers who may be found in their countries, instead of half measures such as the ones contained in the Bill, which are better than nothing.
Let me explain why the Bill is inadequate. If we look at Clause 2, we see that the definition of torture includes any act-and I am skipping to make the point, certainly not to change the meaning-by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for the purpose of punishing that person for an act which he has committed. It is a very good statement, and I think Hon. Members of the House would support it unequivocally. If a person is whipped or beaten, if a person is locked into a freezing room, if a person is buried up to his or her head in the sand, or if a person has a limb amputated, all these things would be permitted under the Act under certain circumstances because of the concluding language in that clause. It says that the definition of torture does not include any act or omission arising only from, inherent in, or incidental to lawful sanctions. We do not need that reservation in Canada. We do not mean to say that an act in which severe pain or suffering, mental or physical, is inflicted for the purpose of punishing a person will be acceptable, if it is incidental to, inherent in, or arising only from lawful sanctions.
There are states which specifically, deliberately, and officially torture people by way of punishment. I was not at the
Criminal Code
United Nations when the treaty was negotiated, but I say sincerely that I assume we tried to eliminate that type of practice in every country. I would assume we tried to make the convention one which would eliminate that. We succeeded to a point, and that is why I am approving the convention on behalf of my Party. However, I urge the House to eliminate the additional language which would qualify certain kinds of torture and make them justified. I do not think they should be.
In our own country and in our own Parliament where we have control of exactly what we will do in the way of ratifying and carrying forward the noble goal of the abolition or elimination of torture, I hope that when I move my amendment it will find favour.

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to say a few words on the legislation before us and to add my thoughts to the whole question of torture, not simply from a domestic perspective in terms of what goes on in Canada, but from a more global perspective.
It has been quite some time now, but I visited Chile for a couple of weeks. Meeting with people who had been tortured and who lived in such a state taught me some lessons about torture. It is important for Canadians to understand what torture is and for our Government to have a serious global commitment to the elimination of torture.
Torture has to do with democracy and dictatorship. It has to do with a Government being at war with its people. It has to do with living in fear and a Government using torture, using all of the powers available to the state to keep people in line to preserve an unjust regime. Torture has to do with injustice, not only a lack of political freedom and a lack of freedom of the press but also when a society is characterized by social and economic injustice. I saw this in Chile. People are living in poverty the likes of which we do not know here. For the unemployed there is no social safety net, no welfare to keep body and soul together. Families have to go without food. People live in shacks that bear no relationship to what a house is like. This is the context in which we must see torture. Torture is part of an unjust society. It is an instrument that a Government uses to impose its will upon its people.
Any effort that our Government can make in the direction of eliminating torture from this planet is worthwhile. How easily the Government, as many of my colleagues have pointed out, could have gone further. We need to go further. However, it is important for Canadians to appreciate just what torture is in real terms. I wanted to share my experience with Canadians about what I learned of torture by visiting a country like Chile, whose citizens are tortured for speaking out and for calling for action to meet the people's basic human needs. I met with individuals who lived through that and still had the courage to go on, were still part of the human rights organization and who spoke out against the lack of freedom and injustice.

March 26, 1987
Adjournment Motion
It is crucial that whatever Canada can do to support people who are fighting against political repression that we do everything we can.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak briefly in support of the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre. The reference at the top of page 3 to any act or omission arising only from, inherent in or incidental to lawful sanctions significantly weakens the protection included in the previous part of the provision. As I read them, those words qualify both subclause (a) and subclause (b) of the definition of torture. This would mean that if an individual intentionally inflicted severe pain or suffering on another individual for the purposes which are set out in subclause (a), that would be permitted if it arose from lawful sanctions.
Surely no lawful sanction should be accepted in Canada which would have as its result the infliction of severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, for the purpose referred to in the definition of torture. I cannot imagine how under any circumstances such acts or omissions would be considered acceptable in any civilized society. For that reason, I would hope that the Government would be prepared to accept the amendment of my colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre.
I might just note as well that while certain incidents of the nature referred to in this Bill are, fortunately, rare in Canada, from time to time there have been allegations of serious wrongdoings including the possibility of torture as defined in
March 26, 1987

the Bill. 1 recall, for example, visiting Archambault Penitentiary in August 1982 and meeting at that time with prisoners who made very serious allegations of the infliction of physical and mental torture upon them. Unfortunately, those allegations were dismissed by the Solicitor General of the day who suggested that the individuals in question should press charges in court if they felt they wished to proceed with the matter. That Solicitor General, of course, sits today as the Hon. Member for York Centre. It was only after a number of independent investigations including an investigation by Amnesty International, an investigation by the International Federation of Human Rights and an investigation by the very respected Moderator of the United Church of Canada that it became clear that there was indeed a very serious possibility of grave wrongdoing, injustice and possibly the infliction of physical and mental torture on prisoners at Archambault. To this day, there has been absolutely no justice whatsoever rendered in that case.
While we certainly support the provisions of this legislation, I would note that it is important that these provisions apply at all levels within Canadian society including Canadian prisons. I would seek clarification from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice on the circumstances in which it might possibly be considered lawful to impose torture flowing from, inherent in or incidental to otherwise lawful sanctions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must tell you that the amendment suggested by my colleague is well intended. That is beside the point, except that we are here to ratify an international convention by way of a Canadian Bill. This is what matters. I appreciate that the Hon. Member is asking us Canadians to go further than the international convention, but if we go further than that Convention, we will put other countries to which we promised concurrence in a situation that may be awkward for some of them. It is not without reason that the United Nations took ten years to reach a consensus on that convention. And I know for having attended the United Nations 40th session from beginning to end how difficult it is internationally to reach a consensus, and how much each detail is significant. I cannot visualize that Canada, which is committed to ratifying that international convention, would add an item that has been discussed in the United Nations, that has been extensively discussed and debated and the inclusion of which found no support.
The Convention states at the end of Section 1: "-but does not include any act or omission arising only from, inherent in or incidental to lawful sanctions".
But the latter part of Section 1 also adds that this section is without prejudice to any international instrument or national act that may contain provisions of a wider scope. There are also other arguments for opposing the amendment. Under that convention, we could be obligated to extradite an individual. This means we could find ourselves in a situation where we would have to extradite an individual because we would have gone further than the International Convention and extradited that person to another country that accepted the International
Criminal Code
Convention as it now stands. We therefore have an international responsibility to abide by that unanimous consensus, as other speakers have indicated.
According to the United Nations, the provision should be interpreted broadly, and I think you have there an answer to your questions, those terms should be interpreted broadly according to international law and human rights. That same section-let us not forget we are implementing it by way of an amendment to the Criminal Code, let us not forget that Section 245 of the Criminal Code is still there and also that that amendment should also be interpreted in the light of Section 245 of the Criminal Code. Hence, Canadian courts will have to use judicial discretion when interpreting Section 245, when interpreting Canadian law.
In conclusion, I would remind you that Section 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms-because after all that is the basis for all our rights here in Canada-the Canadian Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms states in Section 12:
Everyone has the right not to be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment
or punishment.
A Canadian judge when faced with a situation as described earlier by the Hon. Member will interpret the case on the basis of the Charter and Section 245, and that should be ample. My point is, however, that we must respect this international consensus. We must, although at the United Nations, we could for instance ask the U.N. Commission on Human Rights to review this matter and consider going a bit further, and ask U.N. partners to provide the amendment you desire, but always according to the normal procedure at that level.

The Parliamentary Secretary says and admits that our Charter does not contain similar conditions, in other words, administering cruel punishment cannot be justified according to any clause in the Charter because there is none. Here we have a condition for allowing torture. I would like to ask him just to repeat the second article in the Convention he read to us, or both articles. If I remember correctly, the second article provides that the individual State may go further in its own statutes. It is rather difficult to talk about a document I have not read recently. Perhaps I may ask the Parliamentary Secretary or one of his officials to expand on the article that says "without prejudice to any international instrument or national statute containing provisions that are broader in scope." My question is as follows: If we decide to adopt the Bill with the amendment I am proposing, that is, without the qualifying clause and in the spirit of our Charter, will our ratification obligations allow us to do so?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the second part of article 1 should be interpreted as a definition of assault. So if in Canada, under Section 245, you want to punish assault and battery and this definition goes further than what we are proposing today, obviously that definition of assault will take precedence. I think that is what is meant. In fact, we could amend other provisions in the Criminal Code to make them stricter, without

March 26, 1987
Criminal Code
tinkering with the Bill that ratifies an international procedure. 1 think that is how I would interpret it and that is why I think that at the United Nations this second part was added to article 1.

Mr. Speaker, I find it quite extraordinary for the Parliamentary Secretary to suggest that the Canadian legislation cannot have a broader scope than the consensus reached at the United Nations. Of course, that consensus was reached, and various countries had to compromise to reach it. However in Canada, it rests with us to decide what will be our priorities and our legislation. I will then ask the Parliamentary Secretary to explain very clearly to me what is the intention of the Government because section 2 reads as follows: "-torture does not include any act arising only from lawful sanctions."
Does it mean that if the Government of Canada or any other government decided to provide in the law cruel sanctions which would effectively be a physical or mental torture that such sanctions would be accepted and that there would be no penalty for the enforcement of such sanction in Canada or elsewhere?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides you with all these guarantees. Of course we have the right to legislate in Canada. What I am saying is that it is necessary to take into account the international consensus which was established with Canada's participation and today we have agreed to ratify this Convention. We have the right to legislate, but when we participate in a discussion, join a consensus, and agree to ratify a convention, we have to ratify it as proposed and in a way which will meet our partners' approval. I feel that is the way we will further this issue in the world. Our interest here is as Canadians in Canada but it is also our interest as Canadians to see that there is no torture in the world. In this way, I think we can make progress.
So there is protection under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms for all the situations you mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, it is one thing to say that Section 12 of the Charter would provide protection, but the proposed amendment to Section 6 of the Criminal Code provides that where the person who commits the act or omission is, after the commission thereof, present in Canada, then that individual can be charged in Canada. Let us say that Chile, referred to by my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre, has a system of punishment which we clearly view to be cruel torture, but which is legally sanctioned in that country. If an individual from that country who has participated in the physical or mental torture of someone in there finds refuge in Canada, according to the wording of this Bill as it now stands, because those acts were legal in Chile, and despite the fact they are profoundly unjust, unacceptable and indeed unconstitutional in Canada, that individual is immune from prosecution in Canada. That is the implication of these words.
Can the Parliamentary Secretary explain why we are prepared to accept within our borders the presence of individuals who have clearly committed acts of torture solely because they are defined as legal acts under the laws of the country in which they were committed? Why on earth should we accept torturers in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is that the legitimate sanctions mentioned here will clearly have to be interpreted in the light of international law and the United Nations Charter of Rights.
I suggest this is an adequate guarantee. In this context, the unfair legislation of another country which you mentioned would not be considered legitimate under international law in
Canada.

Mr. Speaker, let us go back to the example given by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). In the case of an individual who committed acts of torture in his own country and who comes to Canada, a person who committed crimes elsewhere, except very special crimes in the area of terrorism, the problem is that, in Canada, there is an escape hatch. He has found a shelter, and his country of origin will not seek his extradition. In this country, we could not punish him, because his crime was committed abroad.
Then, we have an opportunity here to do more to abolish and eliminate torture. If we adopt the amendment as proposed, we have the possibility of finding ways to act against this type of torture. That is a very good example. It could happen easily.
I just want to ask again whether the Parliamentary Secretary wants these torturers to find a shelter, or an escape hatch in our country, when we can take action against that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, there will be not refuge in Canada. Let us take the example of a country that would enact a statute to make torture acceptable and, after torturing people, contacted Canada and told us: "There is a law in our country that says torture is acceptable." Clearly, Canadian courts would not find that a lawful sanction. That is clear. According to the interpretation of Canadian law, international law, international human rights charters, that could never be found lawful. This means that nobody will be able to find refuge here.

Against such charges, the individual could answer that the torture inflicted was justifiable because this arose only from lawful sanctions. This is what he could say. He would have a case, and this is why I want to delete that language.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary a very specific question. This is really the crux of the matter. Consider the case of an individual found in Canada who has committed acts in a third country
March 26, 1987

which we would view as acts of torture, whether they be the infliction of physical or mental suffering. The individual has committed the acts pursuant to laws of that third country. In other words, the acts in question are legal. There are lawful sanctions in the country from which that individual has fled. A Canadian judge would be obliged to find that those acts flow from lawful sanctions because the sanctions in question are lawful in the country from which the individual has fled. There is nothing here which states that if the sanctions are illegal by virtue of international law there can be some sort of escape. The only criterion is whether they are lawful sanctions. If indeed the laws of that third country permit these acts, which we in Canada would view as acts of torture, the judge has no jurisdiction whatsoever. Obviously the country in question will not seek extradition and the individual is free to escape justice.
Does the Parliamentary Secretary not recognize that by including this reference to "flowing from lawful sanctions" he is in fact permitting a very serious escape loophole for individuals who may have committed acts of torture in other jurisdictions?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I for one have confidence in the Canadian judicial system to make the necessary distinctions in that area. I do not think you could give me a specific example of what you just mentioned.
The Canadian courts will interpret this in the light of Canadian law and international law. If the action was committed in another country, the courts will also have to base themselves on international conventions accepted and recognized around the world.
So you already have a safeguard, and I do not foresee any complaints. There are countries we will never hear from, where there will never be any problem. When it comes down to it, we know very well where torture is to be found, where torture is inflicted, and we also know those countries often have laws they should be amending.
We in this country will have no problem with that. Our judicial system will make it easy to fight acts of torture that have been inflicted anywhere around the world by people who seek refuge in Canada. I see no problem with that.

Mr. Speaker, I would then ask the Parliamentary Secretary whether he would be prepared to consider an amendment which would make it clear that any lawful sanctions in question must be in accord with the principles of international law. It would appear that that is what the Parliamentary Secretary is in fact stating, and that it is his hope that our courts would in fact interpret the only acceptable sanctions to be those in accord with the principles of international law. If those words at least were included, that would provide some safeguard and an assurance that we are not dealing with sanctions which are solely lawful according to the country in question but, rather, must be recognized as lawful by the international community of nations. The
Criminal Code
Parliamentary Secretary may wish to consider this and we could certainly come back at an early date to consider the Bill with that amendment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That same suggestion was made at the United Nations, where it was turned down by a group of nations which still wanted to sign, and did sign unanimously that international convention. I will refer you to everything that was said at that time at the United Nations. It is my view that we should pass the Bill now, immediately, ratify the international convention that was unanimously adopted by the nations, in order to give a chance to the largest possible number of nations to participate.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question for my hon. colleague. Is he aware that the torture that goes on in countries such as Chile-and I know this from having visited the country-is lawfully sanctioned? When people seek redress in the courts there is no legal remedy. Chile did not write a piece of legislation which says that it is okay to torture, but torture is lawfully sanctioned. I want to remind the Minister of that.
Why should we have such a provision in legislation in Canada? Surely we are against torture. The Parliamentary Secretary said that we have the protection of the Charter of Human Rights. The Charter of Human Rights also has a qualifying clause saying that whatever is reasonable in a democratic society is acceptable. Perhaps a judge would look at this law and say that since Parliament passed it this is reasonable in a democratic society.
The Minister asks whether we do not have confidence in our courts. The courts are there to interpret laws, not to make them. I ask the Minister to think seriously about this. Does he really want to have an exception in law to a ban on torture in this country?

When the Parliamentary Secretary indicated that the qualifier conformity with international law had been rejected it reminded me that I had mentioned earlier that I worry when the United Nations is unanimous about anything. The worry is that the measure on which it has become unanimous is so watered down by intentional ambiguities, vague language or exceptions, that it permits a measure of comfort to a number of states which I think Canadians would like to deny to those states. We know that the list of states which are entering this treaty and perhaps passing legislation include states in which torture occurs.
That which the Parliamentary Secretary has said has made me more convinced that this is important for us in our own country. I am not saying we should not have signed the treaty because I think we should have signed it. It is a step forward. As well, this legislation, without my amendment, is better than no legislation. It is good, progressive, liberal legislation which our Party supports, but it would be better and would add more to the war against torture if this amendment were made. I

March 26, 1987
Message from the Senate
regret to say that I am more convinced now than I was before we started that the amendment is an improvement and that there is no reasonable excuse for not adding it. I urge him once again, before some of his colleagues, who I know from what I read in the media are not trained seals, to recognize the importance of this amendment and to support it.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Caccia that, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider prohibiting the use of lead solder in sealing cans used for food and beverages.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH USE OF LEAD IN SEALING FOOD AND BEVERAGE CANS
speechtext:
You will recall my earlier reference to the Royal Society's Commission in 1986 on the question of lead in the environment. Lead is a powerful toxin and scientists have concluded that it has adverse effects on several body functions, including the central nervous system and circulatory system. Lead is also believed to affect intelligence, particularly in children, as a result of studies carried out
March 26, 1987

over the years by the Learning Disabilities Association of Canada.
The findings of the Royal Society last fall concluded that women, especially when pregnant, and young children are the most vulnerable groups. The commission recommended that the Government's public health and environmental policy should be to reduce blood lead to its lowest possible level. Our exposure to lead ought to be reduced. Food in cans with a lead soldered side seam can absorb lead. Studies which have been conducted have concluded that acidic foods or beverages such as tomatoes or fruit juices can have as much as ten times more lead than fresh fruit or vegetables. The commission recommended that efforts should be made to accelerate the decline in lead content in food, banning lead soldered seams on cans as quickly as possible.
As you will note, Mr. Speaker, if you go to a food market and buy food in cans, both imported cans of food and cans manufactured in Canada with soldered seams are not regulated. Let me be absolutely clear on this and quote from the excellent book written by Barbara Wallace and Kathy Cooper entitled The Citizen's Guide to Lead. If one wants to be sure when buying food in a can that it is safe, one would want to look for a can with no seams at all. If the can has no seams it is safe; it is leadfree. One can always detect if there is a seam even if there is paper wrapped around the can by scratching with a fingernail. If there is a thin blue or black line running along the seam, that food can is leadfree and therefore it is all right. However, if it does not show a blue line or a black line along the seam, then it has been soldered with lead and therefore it is not desirable or advisable to purchase that type of canned food.
Of course, I am not suggesting that all the sources of lead are from canned food. There are a number of occupations that put men and women in touch with lead, people who have to pay particular attention to the presence of lead. I will quickly mention only a few. They are: auto mechanics and automobile workers, cable makers, dental technicians, electroplaters, electrotypers, gasoline blenders, insecticide makers and insecticide users, jewellers, lead miners and lead smelter workers, linoleum makers, solderers, of course, varnish makers, wallpaper printers, and so on, just to mention a few.
It is important that we also remember that one of the largest single sources of environmental lead is the emissions from cars, cars that use leaded gasoline. Over the years the Government has moved in the direction of reducing the content of lead in gasoline, but we still have a certain distance to travel to the day when all the gasoline that will be used and made available both to light vehicles as well as to heavy ones will be free of lead.
At the present time we face a very disturbing situation with motorists who are misfueling their cars. I refer to owners of cars that should be running on unleaded gasoline who tend to buy gasoline which is leaded because it costs less, in spite of
Canned Food and Beverages
urgent signals that many of us have given to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) urging him to change the federal tax on gasoline. Nevertheless, there is an increasing gap in the price between the two gasolines.
Those motorists who are misfueling, namely, those buying gasoline that is leaded for cars that should be running on unleaded, are carrying out a practice that is illegal, as well as doing something which is unhealthy and unfair to the rest of society. We know that the Government has urged motorists to abandon the practice of misfueling gasoline. That campaign has been carried out through the use of advertisements. However, those advertisements will have only limited impact, although I hope they will have some impact, since so long as there is a price differential in gasoline we will be facing this type of problem on the part of motorists who will be tempted to misfuel.
We eat food and we breathe air that contains lead. We have food contaminated by lead fall-out from the atmosphere. It comes back to us by way of coal-fired power plants, by way of cars and trucks using leaded gasoline, as I mentioned before, by factories using heavy fuels and also by way of smelters. We can also have an intake of lead by way of canned food or drink that is canned where lead solder is used to seal the can. As I mentioned earlier, acidic food or acidic beverages, such as tomatoes and the like, or fruit juices, seem to indicate a greater incidence in the presence of lead in those foods. Therefore, the Royal Society's Commission on Lead in the Environment concluded that within the human body lead can lead to a number of difficulties which I have already mentioned.
Returning to my motion, I would, through you, Mr. Speaker, call on the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to take measures that will ban lead soldered seams on cans, which in itself would be a major step forward. Also, the same Minister through his offices must ensure that the importation of cans with lead soldered seams that contain food be brought to a stop.
Finally, it is encouraging to know that the domestic canning industry is gradually replacing cans with lead soldered seams, but that is not enough. The Minister of National Health and Welfare should accelerate this phase-out, particularly with respect to imported canned foods, for the reasons that I have mentioned and which are so well described in a technical paper in the report to which I have made mention.
In the end you and I will agree, Mr. Speaker, it is the consumer who makes the final decision when choosing what to purchase from the shelf in stores. It is for this reason that I am putting this motion in the hope that the message from the Royal Society will be picked up by the Canadian consumer who can, by refusing to purchase lead soldered canned foods, discourage the use of this type of technology which has proven to be unhealthy in terms of the merits and the advantages of human health in general.

March 26, 1987
Canned Food and Beverages

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH USE OF LEAD IN SEALING FOOD AND BEVERAGE CANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the toxic effects of lead have been known for quite some time. As early as two centuries before the beginning of our era the Greeks and the Romans were aware of the harmful effects of lead, but still they continued to expose themselves to them through foods and beverages, particularly wines.
Over the years, many outbreaks of lead poisoning were traced to lead contaminated foods and beverages.
The industrial revolution which had a worldwide impact around the middle of the 18th century led to wider use of lead and, early in the 19th century, workplace related lead poisoning had become a serious public health hazard.
During that period, the toxic effects of lead on the children of lead industry workers were noticed for the first time. In addition, cases of sterility, miscarriage, stillbirth and premature delivery were common, not only among women working in the lead industry but also among the wives of men working in that industry, not to mention the fact that infant mortality was very frequent among the children of these workers.
Gradually however, thanks to better occupational health standards in the industry, cases of congenital lead poisoning declined sharply.
Between 1930 and 1940 the United States reported many serious cases of lead poisoning among children. Some of these cases were thought to be brain tumours, whereas others were wrongly diagnosed as being acute abdominal attacks, which required unnecessary surgery.
The number of deaths due to lead poisoning was extremely high, but some health professionals mistakenly thought that the effects of lead poisoning tended to wear off, without serious consequences.
Two researchers, Byers and Lord, published an eloquent rebuttal of this erroneous concept in 1943, and their book has become a classic on the subject.
They observed that this view, although very widespread, did not take into consideration the effects of lead poisoning on the growth and development of the nervous system of children.
They followed the cases of twenty children who had been cured of lead poisoning and found that all except one did poorly in school.
Most of these children had various behavioural problems, including very short attention spans and impulsive behaviour patterns.
Their study was probably the first to infer that low-dose lead poisoning could lead to subtle behavioural changes and other neurological problems. However, there were no clear signs pointing to a deficiency in the central nervous system.
From the early fifties until the mid-sixties, public health workers alerted to the problem in many major cities in the United States learned to recognize cases of lead poisoning
when it became clear that many children were suffering from this condition.
They found hundreds of cases. Between 1950 and 1960, for instance, 611 cases of lead poisoning and 48 deaths associated with this condition were recorded in Baltimore. Similar surveys were also carried out in New York, Philadelphia and Chicago.
Because of the interest shown in this problem, an increase in the number of cases diagnosed was invariably recorded, as well as a decrease in the seriousness of the affliction. A consistent picture emerged from the data collected by these cities during that period.
Lead poisoning in infants affected nearly exclusively children between the ages of one and six living in run-down housing in large unsanitary urban areas. Smaller children between the ages of one and three were more at risk than older children. The main sources of exposure in such housing were pealing lead-based paint and cracked lead-soaked plaster.
The affliction occurred throughout the year, but the symptons were most common during the summer months. In the absence of adequate building codes or a proper application of existing regulations, the dangers associated with lead-based paint were seldom corrected, which meant that lead poisoning continued to be widespread.
In the mid-sixties came a new social awareness with the discovery of lead poisoning, an avoidable affliction which had reached epidemic proportions in many unsanitary urban areas throughout the world. Moreover, thousands of children who showed no evident sign of sickness were found to have high lead concentrations in their blood. These findings brought health care professionals to recognize the importance of detecting not only an excessive absorption of lead in children to prevent symptomatic poisoning, but also the toxic effects of lead in youngsters.
While lead-based paint used in millions of homes remains the main source of concentrated lead to which children living in run-down housing are exposed, the frequency of an excessive absorption of lead by young children living outside these zones who could be described as rich resulted in a more detailed examination of the possible sources of this substance in the early seventies.
Other sources of exposure were in fact detected at the time: pottery covered by lead-based glazes, leaded gasoline and lead sealed food and soft drink cans.
The seventies also saw a substantial number of discoveries and new technologies. The world came to understand better the metabolism of lead in the human body and the influence of various nutritional factors on lead absorption and toxicity.
Among the major discoveries, I should mention the documentation of substantially higher rates of lead absorption and retention by the gastrointestinal system of children, as well as the fact that children are more sensitive to lead toxicity.
March 26, 1987

Studies carried out during the same period on laboratory animals also showed that long term exposure to weak concentrations of lead could result in behavioural deficiencies.
The United Nations Joint Committee on Food and Agriculture and the World Health Organization, which includes experts on food additives, reviewed the question of lead and its toxicity at its thirtieth meeting in Rome last June.
At a previous meeting held in 1972, this committee had set provisionally the tolerable daily dose of lead at 50 micrograms per kilogram of body weight. The admissible weekly intake, Mr. Speaker, is the maximum amount of lead that a person can ingest in a week without any sign of adverse effect. The committee had mentioned then that it did not apply to children. Due to the particular concern about children and infant health, the committee assembled in 1986 tried to assess the dangers associated with lead in those age groups.
The committee reviewed carefully all available data on that subject. Considering that a daily intake of 3 to 4 micrograms of lead per kilogram of body weight did not cause any increase in blood levels in children and infants, a provisional admissible weekly intake of 25 micrograms of lead per kilogram of body weight was established.
Exposure to lead comes from many sources and lead-soldered cans are only one of the possible sources of contamination.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has provided other federal departments and provincial organisations with particular information on health risks associated with exposure to lead and recommended to limit, as much as possible, exposure to that substance. To that end, federal and provincial levels of Government have passed measures to limit exposure to lead.
Limits have been set for lead in a variety of products such as paints, pesticides, solder for kettles, glazing material for ceramics, especially when used for food.
Regulations have also been passed regarding emissions by lead smelting operations. Moreover, the Department of National Health and Welfare is supporting all initiatives to reduce or eliminate lead in gasoline.
Over that period it has been further established that nutrition was the main source of direct lead exposure for the general population, that is, people who are not exposed at work.
It has also been confirmed that lead-soldered seams was an important source of lead contamination in canned food.
Based on those discoveries, Mr. Speaker, experts in the Health Protection Branch of the Department met with representatives of the canned food industry. Their discussions led to a co-operative, Government-industry program aimed at effective, orderly reduction of lead rates in food.
Canned Food and Beverages
Since it has been established that babies and infants were more sensitive than adults to the toxic effects of lead, regulations have been passed to limit lead rates in canned milk products.
In this way, lead rates in those products could be reduced to concentrations near natural levels. Moreover, other baby foods are no longer sold in lead-sealed containers, and they now include negligible amounts of lead.
Finally, regulations have been made with the aim of limiting the permissible amount of lead in a whole range of foods, including fruit juices, other drinks and more recently, tomato products.
That co-operative effort is on-going and other regulations will be passed where needed to limit the admissible lead concentrations in food.
In an effort to identify any area that could cause problems in that area, the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare is implementing an on-going monitoring program under which its Canadian and imported products experts look for signs of lead contamination.
What has been found is a constant reduction of lead rates in canned foods since the introduction of the program, to such an extent that the lead contamination from that source is now well below tolerable limits established by the Joint Committee of Food Additive Experts.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, I feel there is no need to forbid generally lead sealing of cans.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH USE OF LEAD IN SEALING FOOD AND BEVERAGE CANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to address the resolution introduced by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). As well, it was a pleasure to listen to the very carefully prepared written notes provided by the bureaucracy to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary so that she could exercise her indirect expertise on the subject of the history of lead poisoning in humans.
Of course we know that lead poisoning is a well-known phenomenon. In fact, if the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary had chosen the correct writer for her speech, she would have found in documents of the Department of National Health and Welfare the record of the effects of lead poisoning even in Roman times. Upon the exhumation of corpses in Pompeii, the skeletons were revealed to contain immense quantities of lead, and therefrom arose the theory that perhaps the downfall of Rome is largely attributable to the wide occurrence of lead poisoning among the Romans. Indeed, it has been suggested that the peculiar behaviour of Nero when fiddling while Rome burned and other peculiarities of behaviour among Roman emperors were attributable to their being victims of lead poisoning. If one speculates on the behaviour of presidents, one might perhaps speculate that lead poisoning is not a dead issue

March 26, 1987
Canned Food and Beverages
insofar as its modern effect on the behaviour of national leaders is concerned,
I have listened with interest to the document read by the Parliamentary Secretary. We have had a nice discourse on lead poisoning, its history, its sources and so on. What we have before us today is a proposal to eliminate lead solder welds on cans. It may be argued that to a very large extent regulations have been introduced which limit the extent of lead poisoning. Lead poisoning is not only a serious form of pollution, but a dangerous form of pollution even when it is present in small quantities or low concentrations.
Let me review the effects of lead. The significant toxic effects are on the synthesis of hemoglobin, on renal function and on neurological development, manifesting itself in blood dysfunctions, in aminoaciduria, in glycosuria and neurological impairment. If, during their development, children are exposed to lead, neurological impairment is experienced which manifests itself in difficulty in understanding, in retardation to some degree and on their emotional development. All of this is well documented, and it leads to the conclusion that the effects of lead are so subtle that we should not tolerate any presence of lead in circumstances where it is unnecessary.
The premise of the resolution of the Hon. Member for Davenport is very simple. It is a premise that has been adopted by all of those concerned with environmental pollution. Where it is possible to eliminate sources of pollution, those sources should be eliminated.
One may argue that the regulations already introduced have provided a fair measure of safety. To some degree, that is true. With respect to acid foods where the quantity of lead is to some degree regulated, regulation is not enough. When canned tomatoes, pickles or even a can of milk that has soured are exposed to air, oxidation occurs and lead is spread into the contents. Unless we are prepared to have indicated on every can of food that once opened that can should not sit because it will become acid, then one should approach the problem another way. How many of us open a can of Campbell's Tomato Soup after reading the label carefully? Most of us just open it up, throw the contents in a pan, add milk or water and sugar and eat it, not paying very much attention to what it says thereon.

speechtext:
It is not as if the gentleman from Davenport is suggesting something revolutionary and difficult. There is abundant literature, not only on substitute containers for preserved foods but abundant literature on how to seal a can without using lead.
What we have here, with all due respect to my dear colleague, is not a revolutionary proposal but one that I am sure will come as a surprise to the Hon. Parliamentary
Secretary, dependent as she is for her notes from the bureaucrats who will defend their past works. There are welding seals, plastic seals and cans without seals at all that can be substituted and so provide an extra margin of safety. Then we could add to the efforts, so far successful in some areas, in cutting down the amount of lead poisoning in the environment to those other measures that have been taken.
But it is the same in this example as in everything else with the Government. Canada is still far behind the United States in regulating the use of leaded gasoline. Somehow we cannot come to grips with changes, or even meet the standards which the Americans have already adopted. Now we have a simple proposal that would not be dismissed in any other context: where there is a source of pollution, eliminate the source and then you will not have to bother about the statistics or the scientific evidence that may be doubtful, because when in doubt, be safe. To be safe, the simplest answer is to take the simplest course-whether immediate or phased, eliminate lead from cans.

speechtext: I did, but I wrote my own speech.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   HEALTH USE OF LEAD IN SEALING FOOD AND BEVERAGE CANS
speechtext:
The Member did not say which country it was, but he suggested there was a certain president somewhere who might be suffering from lead poisoning. Could he tell us who that president is and what is going to happen in the future? Will the president go the way he suggested? Will it result in the fall of the an empire? I would suggest the Member might read history and rewrite history as he wanted to suggest today.
The Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, recognizing the potential health hazard to Canadian consumers from lead contamination of canned foods, initiated a co-operative program in 1975 with the food canning industry to reduce lead levels in canned foods. One of the options considered in 1975 was a complete ban on the use of the lead soldered can, as is now proposed in the motion before us. This option, however, was not considered viable and was rejected in 1975 in favour of an orderly and cooperative approach aimed at reducing lead contamination of canned foods. This approach involved regulatory initiatives by the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, together with improvements in lead soldered canned technology and gradual conversion to alternate technologies by the industry.
Why was the banning of the lead soldered can not considered a viable option? The lead soldered can has been the mainstay of the food canning industry since its inception. Not only was the lead soldered can of high physical integrity and
March 26, 1987

durability, the technology for its production and use in the food industry was highly developed, both in Canada and world-wide. Canadian can manufacturers and food processors alike had extensive technical expertise on facilities for the production and use of this canning technique.
While alternative technologies were available, these all had a number of shortcomings which mitigated against the Canadian industry making a radical switch to these techniques in a short period of time. For example, the so-called two-piece can which is drawn from a single sheet of metal and does not require any soldered seams lacked the physical integrity to be produced in the many different sizes and styles required by the food industry.
In addition, to be cost effective, the production of this type of can requires that the production line by operated at least 16 hours per day and that a large volume of one size of can be produced. Because of the relatively small production capacities of the Canadian Food Industry, neither of these requirements could be readily met.
The welded seam can, on the other hand, presented other problems pertaining to its durability, functionality and production which required additional research before its utility in food packaging could be fully determined. Other alternatives such as cemented seams instead of soldered seams, pure tin solders and the like were all considered and found to be fraught with difficulties which prevented them from being immediate viable solutions.
Apart from the technical aspects of these alternate technologies, capital costs as well as operating costs for these new can manufacturing methods had to be considered. It was estimated that conversion to the two-piece can would bear a capital cost investment on the part of the industry of between $1.6 million and $6.4 million per production line with an increased operating cost of $5 to $6 per 1,000 cans. Similarly, the welded-seam can would require a capital investment of about $1 million per line with an increased operating cost of $2.50 to $3.50 per 1,000 cans. These costs had to be compared with the cost of line modification to the existing technology to reduce lead contamination which were of the order of $50,000 per line with an added operating cost of only 20 cents to 30 cents per
1,000	cans.
Conversion to these alternate technologies would not only involve tremendous capital and increased operating costs but could also in certain instances affect jobs. Some food processors in Canada operated their own lead-soldered can manufacturing facilities. Faced with the immediate capital outlay required when switching to different manufacturing methods, these companies might well have decided to discontinue their manufacturing operations and to purchase cans from alternate sources. This could well have resulted in a reduction in these companies' workforce requirements. All of these economic factors would undoubtedly have resulted in substantial increases in the cost of canned foods to Canadian consumers.
Canned Food and Beverages
One other possible repercussion of a ban on the lead-soldered can had to be considered. As I indicated earlier, the lead-soldered can has been the mainstay of the food processing industry for many years and is used world-wide. Canada is a major importer of canned foods. For example, in 1985, more than $300 million worth of canned foods were imported into Canada. A ban on the use of the lead-soldered can by Canadian food processors without a concomitant ban on imported foods packaged in these containers would have resulted in a profound negative impact on the Canadian industry. On the other hand, to ban the importation of canned foods would have been construed as being a non-tariff barrier to trade, contrary to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of which Canada is a signatory.
Bearing in mind the technical difficulties, the potential effects on international trade and the economic consequences of banning the lead-soldered can, it was considered in 1975 that the Canadian consumer could best be served through a program of regulatory initiatives designed to reduce lead levels in canned foods, together with a gradual conversion of the industry to other can manufacturing methods. One might ask if this has been an effective approach. The simple answer to this question is yes. One need only consider, for example, that as a result of this co-operative program between Government and industry, baby foods are now packaged in glass jars, not soldered cans. Consequently, lead levels in such products are in the order of naturally occurring background levels.
In addition, the regulatory initiatives taken by the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare to limit lead levels in certain canned foods, together with improved lead-soldered can-manufacturing techniques, has resulted in significant decreases in lead levels in many canned foods. For example, average lead levels in canned fruit juices prior to the initiation of this program were in the order of .15 parts per million. Today the average lead level in such products is .08 parts per million. Similarly, average lead levels in canned fruits have been reduced from about .3 parts per million to .18 parts per million.
Furthermore, great strides have been made by the canning industry to convert to alternate technologies in an orderly and manageable fashion. In fact, as noted in the recent report to which the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) referred, completed by the Royal Society of Canada, entitled "Lead in the Canadian Environment: Science and Regulations", less than one-third of the 3.5 billion food cans used in Canada in 1985 had lead-soldered side seams. Furthermore, the report noted that by the end of 1986, it was then expected that lead-free cans would account for 95 per cent of Canadian production and use.
To sum up, a ban on the lead-soldered can was not an appropriate or necessary measure in 1975 and it is even less so today. The major steps that have been taken by the Canadian industry, in co-operation with the Department of National Health and Welfare, to convert to new technologies and to limit lead levels in canned foods have resulted in Canadian

March 26, 1987
Adjournment Debate
consumers no longer being exposed to excessive levels of this potentially hazardous metal from canned foods. As the Royal Society of Canada report concluded, food and beverages used to be severely contaminated from solder in cans, but this source has been largely eliminated.
The Hon. Member for Davenport and the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) wanted to get into a discussion of lead in gasoline. The Parliamentary Secretary and I would like to discuss this much further one day, and would like to compare what our Government has done on this subject with what the Liberal Government did. That is a challenge.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate and make a few comments on the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia).
Mr. Speaker, the toxic effects of lead have been indentified for hundred of years now, so much so that everybody is aware of the serious consequences of exposure to massive doses at work or as a result of accidents, for example. However, controversy is focused on the potential hazards of ongoing exposure to weak lead concentrations, especially among children. Many scientists in Canada and elsewhere in the world claim that certain intellectual and behavioural child deficiencies may result from continuous exposure to low lead levels. Such harmful effects are very difficult to pin-point, so it is nearly impossible to prove these theories. But we cannot ignore the fact that exposure to lead concentrations once thought to be harmless may indeed have neurological and behavioural implications.
Lead is a metal which abounds in nature. It is found in soil, air, water and food, usually in very limited quantities. However, as a result of human interventions and activities, this soil, this air, this water and this food may contain much more lead than would otherwise be found in nature.
It has been shown that environmental pollution from mines, smelters and refineries increases the lead content of soil, air, water and food. In addition, the manufacture and use of leaded products, particularly batteries and gas additives, are also sources of lead contamination.
After occupational exposure, the three main sources of exposure for adults are air, water and food.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-FUTURE OF RURAL POST OFFICES
CANADA POST CORPORATION-FUTURE OF RURAL POST OFFICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure if you know where Aylesbury, Saskatchewan, is but I am sure that you and many others across Canada have heard about it during the past few months. Aylesbury is one of the 33 towns in Saskatchewan which since 1985 have had their post office closed.
I would like to give the House a bit of an idea of what Canada Post was like about 20 years ago. It was a Canadian institution ranked at about the same level and with about the same amount of respect as the RCMP or the Canadian flag. It was cost effective, had many dedicated workers and, believe it or not, delivered the mail on time. Under the previous Government all of that fell apart. Billions of dollars were spent on technology which displaced workers but did not work.
Canada Post went from an institution operating on a breakeven basis to incurring an annual deficit of over $500 million. That in turn led to the start up of a lot of courier operations in competition. When the Post Office became a Crown corporation it really did not improve much. Making it a Crown corporation would supposedly remove the political interference that occurred when it was operated by a Minister of the Crown. It did not really work out that way.
People have to voice their concerns and vent their frustrations somewhere about something like this, so they appealed to the only people they knew, their elected Members of Parliament. In Aylesbury, Saskatchewan, people were justifiably and understandably upset when their post office was closed. One of the first things that would happen as a result was that Aylesbury would disappear off the map. Families who had been getting their mail in Aylesbury for three generations would no longer be able to do so. The people protested to Canada Post and to me. I took up their concerns. We finally got Canada Post to agree that these people would still be able to get their mail addressed to Aylesbury even though it would go to either one of two nearby towns. When we indicated that was not good enough, we were told the Post Office would provide green boxes for incoming and outgoing mail. Provision would be made for a stamp agency in town. This was only as a last resort and after the residents of Aylesbury had understandably kicked up quite a fuss.
These people understand the need for restraint and fiscal responsibility. We all understand that. Everyone makes that kind of decision in the operation of their business or household every day. We know we must live within our means. Yet look
March 26, 1987

at the deficit of $123 million which Canada Post is going to try and eliminate by 1987-88. Compare that to the few thousand dollars lost at the Aylesbury Post Office. It is nothing in comparison. Rural residents are understandably upset.
Canada Post does not seem to realize that the post office is more than a place where you get your mail. It is a social gathering spot in small towns. Everyone goes there in the morning to pick up their mail and they meet their friends and visit with each other there. It is a very important part of rural Canada. Then look at the fact that Canada Post has a president and 14 vice-presidents paid, we are told, in the neighbourhood of $120,000 a year. People find it difficult to understand why we need 14 vice-presidents in a Crown corporation when we have only 10 provinces. People look at the absentee rate in the Post Office. Two years ago the big sorting plants had an average absentee rate of 25 days. Twenty-five days is five weeks out of a year. Although that has now dropped to 16 days a year, it is still too high.
Those are the concerns of the people of Aylesbury. The Mayor of Aylesbury, Mr. Hank Watkins, decided to get active to save his post office. He kept the fight up himself as long as he could and then joined up with Rural Dignity. On January 25, 1987, they had a meeting in Aylesbury which the President of Rural Dignity of Canada, Mr. Gilles Raymond of Quebec, attended. Over 200 people from Aylesbury and towns all over Saskatchewan came to the meeting to voice their concerns. They have brought their concerns to Ottawa by appearing before the standing committee. We now have the assurance of the Minister responsible for Canada Post (Mr. Andre) that Members of Parliament will be notified when post office closures are contemplated. We will then discuss that in the communities.
That is what the people want. They want meaningful discussion and to be able to present their concerns to Canada Post and be assured that Canada Post understands them. The people understand that small post offices which have only a very minimum number of boxes will have to be closed. On behalf of the people of Aylesbury that is the plea I want to make to the Minister responsible for Canada Post.
