speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-FUTURE OF RURAL POST OFFICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the new Minister responsible for Canada Post (Mr. Andre) said the other day in the House- you may recall, it was Wednesday, February 18-in the past weeks and months some Members of the Opposition have not been very objective in their statements and questions on the Canada Post Corporation. Mr. Speaker, in so doing, they have helped to cause considerable concern among Canadians in rural areas with respect to the future of postal services in those areas. Mr. Speaker, one Member even went so far as to ask whether Canada Post was going to drop a plan to close 1,700 rural post offices.
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post never intended to proceed with wholesale closing of rural post offices. Furthermore, when the President of the Canada Post Corporation, Mr. Don Lander, appeared before the Standing Committee on Government Operations on November 20, 1986, he referred to Canada Post's plan to have more, not fewer outlets in the future. This is what he said, Mr. Speaker, and I quote: "The net result of our representation plan will be that Canadians will be provided with more outlets in more convenient locations, and at more convenient hours, at less cost to the postal user."
Canada Post will introduce changes in the course of the next ten years and after, turning over the majority of its retail services to the private sector. Generally speaking, private sector outlets have lower operating costs because they are often located on premises where other, non-postal products are already being sold. Canada Post plans to upgrade the service enjoyed by Canadians by improving access to its products and services, putting its outlets in more convenient locations, extending business hours and relying more on the private sector.
The Corporation has now approximately 8,000 sales outlets, with twenty-five per cent of them privately operated as auxiliary post offices. The other sales outlets are operated by the Corporation itself under different guises and are staffed by Corporation employees. The current sales outlets were established over a long period of time and generally speaking, they have not progressed with population growth and business development.
Rural Canada is not the only one affected, Mr. Speaker. The rationalization and streamlining of postal services is also occurring in major centres. The Corporation's plans provide for an increase in the number of sales outlets where the public can buy stamps and other goods and services. Furthermore, there are plans to extend service hours to the public.
Moreover, Canadians in rural areas can be assured that no change will be made without public consultation. The Corporation will give a 90-day advance notice, thus ensuring sufficient time for the Corporation to explain its move and for the community to make its response known. You may rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that we will take due note of this response.
Rural service will improve. The purpose here is not so much to close down post offices as to open new avenues for providing service.
In short, Mr. Speaker, Canada Post Corporation projects for the next ten years should not be cause for alarm, doubts or concern about postal service in Canada. During that ten-year period or more, the Corporation will increase and not reduce the total number of sales outlets for its goods and services in urban and sub-urban communities as well as rural ones. Moreover, due to the fact that the hours of opening will be different and the sales outlets better located, the users will have better access to the Corporation's services.

March 26, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Finally, Canada Post Corporation intends to consult residents of a community before making any change whatsoever and, to this end, it will give at least a 90-day advance notice to Members of Parliament and users of postal services when changes are being considered.

subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF PATENT ACT-COST OF DRUGS. (B) REQUEST FOR PUBLICATION OF STUDIES
PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF PATENT ACT-COST OF DRUGS. (B) REQUEST FOR PUBLICATION OF STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to make a few remarks on the Government's proposed legislation to Canada's Patent Act as it applies to pharmaceutical drugs.
On several occasions I have asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) what those changes will mean to Canadian consumers if the legislation is indeed adopted by Parliament. I have also asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) the same question several times. To date I have not received a satisfactory answer from either Minister.
Canadian consumers do not know what the exact cost of these changes will mean to them. Provincial Governments, which in many instances provide free coverage for those over 65 years of age and for people on fixed incomes, do not know what the additional cost will be to them either. For a party that was elected on a promise to bring more honesty and openness to Government in its relations with Canadians and provincial Governments, it is sure going about it in a strange way.
The Government has also denied repeatedly that this proposal is not part and parcel of the free trade negotiations with the United States. Recent documents have shown that the Government has been less than forthright with Canadians on this matter as well.
You will be interested to know that I have a copy of a report from the office of the United States Trade Representative called the 1986 Report on Foreign Trade Barriers. In this report is a discussion of the Canadian Government's Bill to change the Patent Act regarding pharmaceutical drugs. Under the section of the report entitled "Compulsory Pharmaceutical Patents Licensing", there are three items. The first is a U.S. description of the Canadian legislation. It states:
Section 41 of Canada's patent law says any company may request the Canadian Patent Commissioner to provide a compulsory licence for pharmaceutical patents. It also requires only a nominal 4 per cent royalty payment. Although a similar provision dates back to World War 1, this section was enacted in 1969 after assertions that foreign pharmaceutical companies were making inordinately high profits in Canada.
The measure was based on a subsequently repealed British patent law. It was designed to rectify perceived problems and foster greater pharmaceutical industry competition. The law is highly popular.
He means that the law is highly popular in Canada. It continues:
On May 27, 1983, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs announced Canada's decision to change Section 41 and launch extensive discussions with provincial governments, the pharmaceutical industry and consumer groups to stimulate the Canadian pharmaceutical industry and maintain reasonably priced drugs.
More than 150 applications for compulsory licences were filed following the May 1983 announcement of a possible change in the law. U.S. officials indicated any legislative change needs to take these applications into account.
That I find rather strange. It goes on to say:
In June 1986 Canada announced the terms of legislation it will introduce in late fall 1986 to modify Canada's patent law.
The person goes on to say:
This proposed bill is being reviewed to see whether it would provide acceptable patent protection standards.
Acceptable to whom? In this case the United States Government is saying it would have to find Canada's legislation acceptable to its interests. Under the heading "Estimated Impact" he estimates that these practices which have existed in Canada since 1969 cost U.S. pharmaceutical interests significant lost revenues each year. Under the heading "Actions Taken or To Be Taken", he goes on to say the United States continues to raise its concerns at senior government levels. It urges speedy submission of modifying legislation to address serious U.S. concerns about the inadequacy of Canadian patent protection in this area.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs continually stands in this House and tells us that no officials from the United States Government have approached them to have any influence on Canada's patent laws. I find the statements made by this representative of the U.S. Government to be totally in contradiction and, indeed, in conflict with what the Minister has been saying in an effort to try to convince Members of the House, and the Canadian public, that this law is being changed in the Canadian interests. Clearly, the document to which I have just referred shows that the legislation is not being changed in Canadian interests. It is being changed simply because the President of the United States has demanded that Canada change it as a precondition to trade negotiations commencing and also to ensure the multinational pharmaceutical industry a higher degree of profit at the expense of Canadians.
I want to say, as I have said before, that Canadians are going to pay an arm and a leg as a result of this change in policy, whether through higher drug prices or through higher provincial taxes because these governments give senior citizens, for example, free drug coverage. One way or the other, Canadians are going to pay through the nose for this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-PROPOSED AMENDMENT OF PATENT ACT-COST OF DRUGS. (B) REQUEST FOR PUBLICATION OF STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister replied to the question of the Hon. Member last October 6, he referred to the cost of some 3,000 drugs available on the Canadian market. None of the proposed amendments to the Patent Act should
March 26, 1987

result in a price increase of these products. The price competition engendered by the generic sector will continue under the new policy since generic products now on the market will not be affected by the proposed changes. In addition, Mr. Speaker, the new compulsory licenses will continue to be granted to generic manufacturers as soon as the period of exclusivity for patented products comes to an end.
In addition, the proposed amendments to the Patent Act provide for establishing a Patented Medecine Prices Review Board which will be empowered to review the prices of all patented medecine. If it finds their prices excessive according to its standards, the Board will have the power to impose sanctions to the producers. The Board will then be able to set a reasonable price level. It will also be able to revoke the exclusivity period for the drug in question or any other drug sold by the same producer.
Mr. Speaker, by establishing evaluation criteria for the price of drugs now on the market, the Board will be empowered to consider the price of drugs in the same therapeutic category as that particular drug or similar drugs, the prices set in other countries, manufacturing and distribution costs, the rate of increase in the price of the drug compared with the consumer price index and any other factor which the Board will consider relevant.
In the case of newly marketed drugs, the Board will be empowered to set an entry price by referring to factors similar to those already mentioned. The Patent Act will require each manufacturer to provide the Board with information to make comparative analyses. Failure to do so will be treated exactly the same as the setting of excessive prices. Thus, the Board will be assured of obtaining all the information required to determine whether the price level of drugs is reasonable or not.
Finally, the Bill includes provisions which will allow for reviews of the legislation four years and ten years after its coming into force. Price trends for drugs and the level of industrial benefits will then be analyzed, and adjustments will be made to the original legislation if required.

subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-CONSTRUCTION OF FISHING TRAWLERS- REQUEST FOR CANADA-FIRST POLICY
SHIPBUILDING-CONSTRUCTION OF FISHING TRAWLERS- REQUEST FOR CANADA-FIRST POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to make a few comments about the state of the shipbuilding industry and, in particular, how it could be positively affected in Atlantic Canada. To preface my remarks I wish to express my gratitude to the Canadian Shipbuilding & Ship Repairing Association for providing me with documentation, facts and figures, which I hope will go a long way to presenting a positive case to the Minister responsible and the position that I am taking.
I also want to say that I have had an opportunity to talk with the Minister directly since my question to him of November 20, 1986. At that time I asked him to consider a
Adjournment Debate
built-in-Canada policy for the construction of fishing vessels over 100 feet in length. I am pleased that the Minister has responded from the point of view of being interested in the points that I have brought to his attention, as well as the points which the association has brought to his attention, and others.
At this time I wish to take a few moments to re-emphasize the points that have been made. Hopefully, the Minister will take this as a positive representation and act accordingly. I am very interested to hear what the Parliamentary Secretary has to say in response to my comments.
I do not think it is any secret that the ship repair industry and the shipbuilding industry as a whole in Canada have taken a substantial plummet in terms of employment opportunities and in terms of contributing to the economy of the nation over the past few years. By way of substantiation of these remarks I would like to point out that in December of 1986 employment by association members in the CSSRA reached its lowest level in one-half a century with the employment of only 5,500 people. Just a short six years ago, in 1982, almost three times that number were working. We also saw several shipyards close last year.
There is no question that we are in desperate need of new policies by the Government to encourage and to inject into the shipbuilding industry a new sense of responsibility and opportunity. I would like to suggest that there is one way we can address ourselves to that.
By way of background, I would like to say that in 1955 there was a decision taken by the Government of the day to exempt fishing vessels over 100 feet in length from the normal 25 per cent duty that had been imposed on foreign ship imports into the country. That move was generally based on the fact that at that time Canada had a 12-mile limit on fishing. In order to allow our fishermen to compete with foreign fishermen, it was decided that it would be in the best interests of the fishing industry to not impose that duty of 25 per cent. It became redundant in 1970 when Canada proclaimed its 200-mile limit on fishing.
Since that time there has been substantial interest expressed in this issue by various Premiers. I refer to Premiers Buchanan, Hatfield and Peckford. All three of these Premiers have come out in favour of removing the exemption, as have the Premiers of Prince Edward Island and Quebec.
I think it is important to point out that at the end of 1985 of the 221 vessels that were in service in the Atlantic fishery, on 194 of them we were able to procure an age profile. We can assume that 20 years is the average life of vessels equipped sufficiently to harvest quality catches. A substantial number of those vessels, at least 169 of them, according to that criterion should be replaced over the next 10 years.
However, taking into consideration the likelihood that new vessels will be more efficient and thus fewer of them will be required, and working with an average of 80 vessels to 100

March 26, 1987
Adjournment Debate
vessels, we see that the potential for demand could be substantial if indeed the 25 per cent exemption were eliminated. I am talking in the vicinity of anywhere from $560 million over a 10-year period to in excess of $1.1 billion.
1 want to impress upon the House and the nation that in terms of Atlantic Canada this could mean an average of 2,700 to 5,700 jobs in the period of 10 years, with the majority being in Atlantic Canada. It is very important to that part of the country.
Also, it would have a minimum impact upon the fishing industry. If all things were taken into consideration, it would probably mean that the fish processing costs would not be increased from a low of .89 per cent to a high of 2.83 per cent.
Our major competitor is the United States of America, and 80 per cent of our fish exports go to that nation. All U.S. fishing vessel repairs and conversions done abroad are subjected to a 50 per cent tariff. In view of those facts, it is obvious that we should adopt an open "buy Canadian" policy which would be a tremendous boon to Atlantic Canada and to the people of the nation as a whole.
I urge the Government to take immediate action to impose a policy which would bring Canadian shipbuilding back on to its feet in Atlantic Canada and to address itself to the very serious concerns of that region of the nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SHIPBUILDING-CONSTRUCTION OF FISHING TRAWLERS- REQUEST FOR CANADA-FIRST POLICY
speechtext:
Mr.Speaker, I shall, if I may, respond to the constructive comments made by the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett) with respect to the tariff applicable to large fishing vessels.
The Government is well aware of the very serious problems facing the Canadian shipbuilding industry, and it wants to do everything it can to help the industry in its efforts to remain viable, considering the world-wide slowdown in activity in the shipbuilding sector and the fiercely competitive situation on international markets.
The Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association has made representations seeking implementation of further safeguards. Unfortunately, we are very restricted in the kind of
action we can take on many of these proposals because of our international trade obligations.
One of the requests of the shipbuilders concerns imposing a duty of 25 per cent on large fishing vessels, namely those over 30.5 meters. Smaller fishing vessels are already subject to a duty of 25 per cent. Although the tariff for large fishing vessels has not been consolidated under GATT, I would like to point out that these vessels have been entering this country duty-free since 1955 and that, at this stage, it would be difficult to justify to the fishermen a re-imposition of the tariff, especially at a time when the fishing industry is starting to show signs of becoming viable once more.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) indicated on November 20 last year, this question was considered very carefully in preparation for the 1985 budget. At that time, as many Hon. Members will be aware, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) decided, considering the cost differential between Canadian and foreign vessels, that such a tariff would have put a heavy financial burden on the fishing industry, with no guarantee of benefits for the shipbuilding industry to compensate.
According to the Government, the situation has not evolved to the point that it could reverse the decision it made only two years ago. However, officials have been asked to re-examine the question to confirm that the situation has remained basically unchanged since the 1985 Budget, and this would lead us to believe that the financial burden of such a tariff for the fishing industry would be more than offset by the benefits which the Canadian shipbuilding industry would stand to gain.
Mr. Speaker, I should like in conclusion to emphasize once again that the Government is committed to considering all practical steps that could be taken to help the shipbuilding industry which is experiencing some difficulties, recognizing the importance of that industry for many communities as well as for the national economy.
